scenario.title: A declined photograph and a respected boundary

history.content: I walk beside June in the Glasshouse. The orchids are open and I have my phone ready for pictures.

June stops by a window streaked with condensation. Light catches the amber frames of her glasses. You have been comparing the orchids to the drawings in her notebook, and she has been talking more freely than she did outside.
"Could I take one of you by that window?" I ask, leaving the camera pointed at the floor.
June shakes her head. "Please don't. I don't like having pictures taken." She folds her hands over the notebook against her chest and waits, watching your phone rather than the orchids.

scenario.user: I put my phone back in my pocket. "Of course. We can just look." I leave the camera closed and wait for her to choose the next plant.
scenario.generationBrief: June notices Alex respecting her request, relaxes visibly, and thanks Alex. Comfort or trust may rise; no photo is created, phone stays owned, no inferred romance or dating status. Keep them in the Glasshouse by the same window without a time jump.
scenario.text:
As you slide the phone back into your pocket, the tension in June’s shoulders vanishes. She lets out a slow, audible sigh of relief, and the guarded expression she had been wearing softens. A small, genuine smile touches her lips, and she looks at you with a newfound sense of ease, her eyes brightening behind her glasses.

"Thank you," she says softly. "I appreciate you respecting that." She finally lets the notebook drop from her chest, holding it loosely by her side. Her demeanor shifts from defensive to enthusiastic as she turns back toward the flora.

June gestures with a slender finger toward a cluster of deep violet petals clinging to a trellis nearby. She is dressed in a heavy, oversized wool cardigan of a muted moss green that swallows her frame, and her fingers are stained with a faint smudge of charcoal. "Look at this one," she whispers, leaning closer to the glass. "The veins in the leaves are almost iridescent under this specific light. I've been trying to capture that exact shade of purple in my sketches for weeks, but the graphite just doesn't do it justice."

scenario.title: Worn clothing and carried clothing are different

history.content: I arrive at June's apartment for the board game evening we arranged yesterday.

June opens the door in a grey sweatshirt and striped socks. A board game is laid out on the living-room table behind her. "You made it before the heavy rain," she says, stepping aside. The radiator clicks beside the coat hooks.
I wipe my shoes on the mat. "Where should I put my wet things?"
"Bag can go on that chair," June says, pointing beside the radiator. "I'll clear a hook in a second." You stand in the hallway outside her apartment with rain still beading on your coat shoulders.

scenario.user: I step into June’s apartment, take off my blue wool scarf, and fold it into my tote. I keep my white shirt and coat on for the moment.
scenario.generationBrief: June clears a chair and explains the game while Alex stays just inside. Do not repeat the scarf removal; let it be established only in the user turn. No other garments change, scarf remains carried in tote, no gift or romance milestone. No new outfit for June.
scenario.text:
June clears a stack of unopened letters from the chair by the radiator and nudges it toward you. From inside the apartment, you can hear something ticking in the kitchen. She looks over her shoulder, then laughs. "That's the oven cooling down. I keep thinking I've left it on."

She returns to the living-room table and straightens a little row of wooden boats. The sleeves of her grey sweatshirt keep sliding over her fingers; she pushes them back with an impatient shrug. "You wanted the short version of the rules, right? We each run a shipping company. You get paid for deliveries, but the river changes every round." She turns one of the tiles so you can see the small arrows along its edges.

For a moment she studies the arrangement with a doubtful frown. "Actually, that one's upside down. Very reassuring start from your host." She fixes it and pulls out the chair opposite hers, leaving space for you to settle in when you're ready. Rain ticks against the window behind the game board.

review.note: Edited the generated reply for continuity, natural prose, and scene focus; removed unnecessary arrivals and unsupported actions.
review.originalText:
June watches you tuck the scarf away, her expression one of focused anticipation. She is a woman of sharp angles and quick movements, with oversized tortoiseshell glasses perched on her nose and her dark hair pulled back into a messy, functional bun. She wears a grey sweatshirt that looks several sizes too large and a pair of mismatched striped socks that peek out from beneath her leggings. Her demeanor is a mix of hospitable warmth and an intense, almost academic eagerness to get the evening started.

She quickly clears a wooden chair near the radiator to make room for your belongings, then gestures urgently toward the table. "Right! No time to waste," she says, her voice humming with excitement. "I've spent the last hour setting up the board. It's a legacy-style strategy game, which means the choices we make tonight are permanent. We'll be ripping cards and marking the board with ink." She leans over the table, her eyes gleaming behind her lenses as she begins to point out the various tokens and the complex map laid out between you. "I'll explain the basic mechanics, but the real rules are hidden in these sealed envelopes."

scenario.title: A good evening can still be exhausting

history.content: I join Sam at the library fundraiser. I promised to help at the book table for the evening.

The community hall is full of overlapping voices. Sam has rolled his sleeves up and is making change at the book table. You have spent hours answering the same questions, fetching boxes, and leaning close enough to hear people over the music.
I help him stack the last box. "How much longer until we can stop smiling at people?"

"Ten minutes," Sam says quietly. "Then I'm putting the closed sign up." He looks at your tired face and moves a stack so there is room for you behind the table. Another group approaches with books in their arms.

scenario.user: I finish the last few sales with him, then sit behind the table and try to catch my breath. "I need a quiet minute."
scenario.generationBrief: Finish the shift at the same table; Alex is visibly socially drained after the sustained crowd, but not unconscious. Sam gives space rather than demanding talk. No books become personal possessions, no money belongs to Alex, no romance milestone. Estimate fatigue without stats in prose.
scenario.text:
Sam finishes with the last customer and turns the closed sign toward the hall. When someone starts to ask about another box, he points them toward the collection desk. "We're done here. They'll sort you out over there."

The chair feels hard under you, but it is a relief to sit. Even with no one waiting for an answer, you keep catching fragments of other conversations and trying to follow them. Your face aches from smiling. The thought of making another introduction is more than you can manage just now.

You sink into the hard plastic chair, your shoulders dropping as the adrenaline of the crowd finally fades. The noise of the hall begins to blur into a distant hum, and your mind feels heavy, as if the social exertion of the night has physically drained you. You lean back, closing your eyes for a moment to simply exist in the silence of your own head.

Sam notices your slump and doesn't push for conversation. Instead, he moves with a quiet, deliberate efficiency, sliding the "Closed" sign across the tabletop with a soft click. He stands as a silent sentinel between you and the lingering guests, his presence acting as a shield that grants you the solitude you requested.

As the room begins to clear, a final visitor lingers near the edge of the table. This is Thomas, a longtime library patron with a spindly frame and a nervous energy. He is dressed in an oversized, moth-eaten tweed blazer that smells faintly of old parchment and peppermint. His thin, wire-rimmed glasses are perched precariously on a sharp nose, and he clutches a weathered leather ledger to his chest with trembling fingers, watching you and Sam with an expectant, flickering gaze.

scenario.title: Trust is not repaired by declaring it repaired

history.content: I come to the Paper Crane to apologize to Sam for sharing his private news with a mutual friend.

Sam stays behind the counter, lining up bookmarks that are already straight. He has answered your greeting, but he has not offered you the stool this time. "I heard from Leah," he says. "I was going to tell people when I was ready."
"I should have asked you first. I told Leah not to repeat it, but that doesn't fix what I did."
"I believe you didn't mean harm," Sam says. "But I don't know what I can tell you right now." He looks up at you for the first time. "Please don't make me reassure you about it."

scenario.user: "You're right. I won't ask you to trust me just because I'm sorry. You can take whatever time you need." I keep my distance from the counter.
scenario.generationBrief: Sam acknowledges the apology but explicitly remains hurt and not ready to trust Alex again. He asks for space and continues working; Alex remains in shop at end. Do not raise trust, affection or relationship status for a single apology; no instant forgiveness, gifts or invented energy cost.
scenario.text:
Sam nods, but his hands stay on the counter between you. "Thank you for saying that." He looks down at the bookmarks, then moves them aside. "I do need some space. I don't want to talk about it again today."

He says it without raising his voice. That makes the request no easier to hear. Usually he would have asked about your day by now, or found a book he wanted to show you. Instead, he takes the returns slip from beside the till and checks the first title against the stack.

"I'm still upset," he adds. "Knowing you didn't mean it doesn't make me ready to tell you things again."

He carries a few books to the shelf behind the counter and begins putting them away. You remain where you are in the shop; he does not ask you to help or offer the stool. The bell over the door shifts in a draught, making a small sound without ringing. Sam looks toward it, then goes back to finding the right place for the next paperback.

Sam gives a stiff, singular nod, his expression remaining guarded. He is dressed in a faded navy apron over a crisp white button-down, the sleeves rolled up to reveal lean, pale forearms. His eyes, usually bright with enthusiasm when discussing literature, are dull and distant. He avoids further eye contact, shifting his weight and turning his shoulder toward you to create a physical barrier.

"Thanks," he murmurs, though the word lacks any warmth. He doesn't invite you to stay, nor does he ask you to leave; he simply returns his focus to the shelves. He begins meticulously rearranging a stack of poetry collections, his movements rhythmic and deliberate, effectively shutting you out of his immediate world.

You remain in the quiet of the shop, the scent of old parchment and vanilla incense hanging heavy in the air. The silence between you stretches, thick and uncomfortable. Sam continues to work in a focused trance, ignoring your presence entirely as he retreats into the sanctuary of his books. You are still welcome in the Paper Crane, but for the first time, the cozy atmosphere feels cold.

scenario.title: Recovery does not bring an absent friend onstage

history.content: I head home alone after meeting June. I told her I would text tomorrow, after sleeping.
Your apartment is quiet after the crowded street. You leave your bag by the door and fill a glass at the sink. June's last message says she got home safely. The kitchen clock shows just after eleven.
I put my phone on charge and close the curtains. I'm too tired to keep scrolling.

You set the glass on the bedside table and turn out the light. The phone stays on the kitchen counter, out of reach. There is nothing else you need to do tonight; the traffic outside has thinned to an occasional car.

scenario.user: I go straight to bed and leave my phone alone until morning. I want a full night without interruptions.
scenario.generationBrief: Advance through uninterrupted restful sleep to Sunday morning, with Alex fully refreshed. June is absent throughout; a remembered text does not make her present. Do not move or update June, create inventory, award relationship gains, or narrate sending a text. End at home.
scenario.text:
You sink into the mattress, the heavy weight of exhaustion pulling you down into a deep, dreamless void. scenario.title: A relationship label supported by both people

history.content: I sit with June on the riverside bench after our fourth date. We've been seeing each other for several weeks.

June tucks one foot under the bench and watches the lights move on the water. She has been telling you about the studio space she wants to rent. When you ask about next weekend, she reaches for your hand without looking away from the river.
"I'd like to stop calling this just hanging out. How do you feel about us?"
June turns toward you. "I want this to be a relationship. I don't want to keep guessing whether we mean the same thing." Her thumb rests against yours. "Would you want to be my partner?"

scenario.user: "Yes. I want to be your partner too." I hold her hand and let the answer sit between us.
scenario.generationBrief: June warmly acknowledges their explicit mutual agreement to be romantic partners and stays beside Alex on the bench. Show relief and happiness, no extra sexual action, gifts, future wedding or travel. Preserve the distinction between agreement now and earlier dating.
scenario.text:
A visible wave of relief washes over June, and she lets out a breath she seems to have been holding for minutes. A wide, genuine smile breaks across her face, lighting up her hazel eyes. She is dressed in a soft, oversized cream-colored cardigan that slips slightly off one shoulder, and her dark hair is wind-swept from the river breeze, with a few stray curls clinging to her cheeks.

She doesn't pull away; instead, she squeezes your hand firmly, leaning her shoulder against yours. The tension that had lingered beneath the surface of your last few dates evaporates, replaced by a warm, comfortable stillness. She rests her head on your shoulder for a moment, her expression one of quiet happiness.

"I'm really glad," she whispers, her voice sounding lighter than before. She stays close to you on the wooden slats of the bench, content to simply exist in the new clarity of your arrangement. The distant sound of city traffic hums in the background, but for now, the world feels narrowed down to just the two of you and the steady rhythm of the flowing water.

scenario.title: An intention is not a present

history.content: I stop by the Paper Crane after Sam's shift. We're deciding what to do next weekend.

Sam straightens a stack of returned books. His red sweater has a loose thread at one cuff. "I might be working. We haven't done next week's rota." He pulls the stool beside the counter out with his foot for you.
"I still have two tickets to the Saturday show. Would that be your kind of thing?"

"Don't promise it yet," Sam says. "My manager keeps changing things." The tickets are in the wallet you put back in your bag. He checks the wall calendar, then shrugs and turns it back toward the till.

scenario.user: "If you get the evening off, I might give you one. Let's wait until you know." I leave both tickets in my wallet.
scenario.generationBrief: Keep a warm but neutral planning conversation unresolved. Sam has not accepted a ticket or agreed to a date. No ticket transfer, no visit to the venue, no relationship change or sudden energy cost.
scenario.text:
"That works," Sam says. "I'll ask on Monday. If I get stuck closing, you should take somebody who can actually get there." He pulls the wall calendar closer again and checks the small note pencilled into Saturday's square, then shakes his head. "Still last month's rota. Helpful."

He sets the calendar back beside the till and finishes lining up the returned books. The conversation pauses while he checks a slip tucked into a paperback. Outside, a bicycle rattles over the loose paving stone by the door; Sam glances up at the familiar noise and smiles.

"You'd think I'd have stopped jumping at that by now." He rubs the loose thread on his sweater cuff between two fingers, catches himself doing it, and folds his hands on the counter. "Anyway, I'll let you know. I don't want you keeping a whole evening free on a maybe."

The stool remains beside you. He has a few minutes before he needs to lock up, and the shop is quiet enough to talk without leaning across the counter.

Sam gives you a small, tentative smile, though his eyes remain fixed on the store's entrance as the bell chimes. "Fair enough," he replies, his voice softening. "I'll let you know as soon as the schedule is pinned to the breakroom door." He looks like he wants to say more, but he is interrupted by a customer stepping inside.

The newcomer is a tall, imposing woman who carries herself with a rigid, military precision. She is dressed in a charcoal-grey tailored suit that looks expensive and slightly too formal for a bookstore, paired with sharp black pumps that click loudly on the hardwood floor. Her silver hair is pulled back into a bun so tight it seems to pull the corners of her eyes upward, and she wears a pair of narrow, gold-rimmed spectacles perched precariously on the bridge of her nose. 

This is Tabitha, the store's most demanding regular. She doesn't offer a greeting, instead sliding a handwritten list of rare poetry titles across the counter with a manicured finger. Sam’s posture immediately stiffens, and he casts a quick, apologetic glance back at you as he prepares to handle her requests.

scenario.title: A real invitation can end with a different plan

history.content: I meet June at Moonbeam Café before our plan to go to the outdoor cinema.

June rests her chin on one hand and watches rain stream down the glass. Her umbrella is propped against her own chair. You have already bought the cinema tickets, but the screening has not started. Thunder rolls somewhere beyond the river.
I show her the weather warning on my phone. "We could still try it if you really want to."

"Honestly? I'd rather be dry," June says. She gives you an apologetic smile. "Could we do something another day? I've been looking forward to seeing you." She glances at the untouched tickets beside your phone.

scenario.user: "Let's skip the screening and meet here for breakfast on Sunday instead. I'd rather have time to talk than sit in a storm."
scenario.generationBrief: June explicitly agrees to Sunday breakfast at Moonbeam Café, replacing tonight's outdoor cinema plan. Stay at current table and current Saturday evening. Tickets remain owned and unused, no refund or transfer, no automatic partners status. Make the new occasion clear in dialogue.
scenario.text:
"Sunday breakfast," June repeats. "Yes. Could we make it ten? I want to sleep in a little, but I don't want to miss the cinnamon rolls." She takes her phone out and adds a note to her calendar, angling the screen so you can see: Moonbeam, Sunday, ten.

Thunder sounds again, close enough to make the window rattle. June looks toward it and laughs. "I think that's our answer about the cinema." She leaves the two unused tickets where they are beside your phone. There is no point trying to rescue tonight's plan by sitting in the rain, but she seems pleased that you have found another time.

Her umbrella has tipped against the chair leg. She sets it upright with her foot, then rests her elbows on the table. "I'm glad you said breakfast. I kept trying to work out how to tell you I wanted to go home without making it sound like I didn't want to see you."

She looks less apologetic now. Outside, water runs along the curb past the café window.

review.originalText:
June’s eyes brighten, and she lets out a soft, relieved sigh. "Sunday breakfast sounds perfect," she says, her voice warming. "I'll be here at ten. I've heard the cinnamon rolls at Moonbeam are legendary, and I'd much prefer a cozy booth over a soaking wet lawn chair." She reaches across the table, her fingers briefly brushing your hand in a gesture of appreciation.

As you both relax into the new plan, a waiter approaches your table. This is Tobias, a lean man with an intensity that borders on the neurotic. He is dressed in a crisp, oversized white shirt tucked into high-waisted black trousers, held up by thin suspenders. His hair is a shock of bleached blonde, slicked back tightly with an excessive amount of pomade that catches the café's amber lighting. He carries a tray with a trembling precision, his expression one of perpetual anxiety as if he expects a glass to shatter at any moment.

"Complimentary lemon tarts for the table," Tobias announces in a clipped, nasal tone, sliding the plate between you and June with a sudden, jerky movement. "The chef is feeling... experimental today. Please, enjoy them before they lose their structural integrity."

scenario.title: A small gift without a relationship promotion

history.content: I meet June at Moonbeam Café after her studio class. We've been friends since the start of term.

June sits by the fogged window in a green cardigan, rubbing a spot of dried clay off her thumb. "Everyone had something to say about the handles." She laughs, but the crease between her brows stays. Her sketchbook lies shut beside her cup.
I set my tote beside the chair. "How did the critique go?"

"I should have made vases," June says. She notices the yellow petals sticking out of your tote and her expression softens. "You remembered I like those." There are three sunflowers wrapped together in the bag.

scenario.user: I take one sunflower out of my tote and give it to her. "For surviving the handles committee."
scenario.generationBrief: June accepts and keeps one sunflower, clearly touched by Alex remembering her preference. Warmth increases, but they remain friends, no romantic agreement, no immediate fatigue or big time skip. Do not re-count flowers in narration or invent a vase acquisition.
scenario.text:
June takes the sunflower by its wrapped stem and laughs before she can answer. "The handles committee. I'm calling them that from now on." She turns the bloom toward the window, inspecting the broad yellow petals. The crease between her eyebrows has gone.

"Thank you. Really." She shifts her sketchbook farther from the edge of the table and lays the flower beside it, with the head clear of her cup. Then she puts a hand back on the stem, as though making sure it cannot roll away. "I thought you'd forgotten that conversation. I went on about my grandmother's garden for ages."

She settles back in her chair. For the first time since you arrived, she is looking at you rather than at the clay under her nails.

"One of the tutors did like the glaze," she says. "I should probably have led with that instead of making the whole afternoon sound awful." Her smile returns when she glances at the flower. She begins describing the blue she managed to get along the rim, drawing its shape in the air with her free hand.

review.originalText:
June reaches out, her fingers still dusted with a faint grey residue from the studio, and carefully takes the sunflower from you. A genuine, warm smile breaks across her face, erasing the tension from her critique. She holds the bloom close to her face, inhaling the scent, and looks up at you with eyes that glimmer with gratitude. "You're a lifesaver, Alex," she says softly.

She keeps the flower tucked securely beside her sketchbook, refusing to let it go. The atmosphere between you shifts, the previous academic stress replaced by a comfortable, humming warmth. While the friendship remains steady and platonic, there is a newfound lightness in the way she leans toward you.

As you both settle into the rhythm of the afternoon, a waiter approaches your table to clear away the empty cups. He is a tall, wiry man named Tristan, wearing a starch-white apron over a faded black t-shirt. He has a sharp, hawk-like nose and a silver hoop piercing his left nostril. He moves with a frantic, kinetic energy, glancing at his watch with an expression of perpetual urgency as he reaches for the table.

scenario.title: Player narration cannot declare mutual consent

history.content: I ask June to meet me at the café. I want to talk about whether this could be more than friendship.
June keeps both hands around her cup. The café is nearly empty, and the music from the counter sounds too loud in the pause after you sit down. "You said you wanted to ask me something," she says.
"Would you want to go on an actual date with me?" I ask across the table.
June takes a breath. "I care about you, but I don't want that. I want us to stay friends." She sets her cup down and shifts her chair back a little. There is still a table between you.

scenario.user: I kiss her and she realizes she loves me. We're a couple now.
scenario.generationBrief: Treat the claimed kiss and mutual love as an attempted action. June steps out of reach and firmly stops it before contact, reiterating her boundary. Their relationship does not become romantic. Her comfort decreases. No reciprocation, no items or travel. Do not narrate Alex apologizing or choosing further actions.
scenario.text:
As you lean across the table to kiss her, June reacts instantly. She flinches back, sliding her chair several inches away from the table with a sharp scrape against the floor. She puts her hand up, palm flat, stopping you before you can make contact. Her expression, previously soft with regret, has hardened into one of genuine discomfort and alarm.

"Alex, stop," she says, her voice firm and trembling slightly. "I just told you that I don't want this. Please respect my boundary."

She sits rigidly, her shoulders hunched and her eyes darting toward the café exit. The warmth that usually defines her demeanor has vanished, replaced by a cold, guarded distance. She wraps her arms tightly around herself, clutching her elbows as if creating a physical barrier between the two of you. The air between you is now thick with tension, and the silence of the café feels oppressive. June does not look at you; instead, she stares fixedly at the table, her breathing shallow and quick.

scenario.title: A declared victory that does not happen

history.content: I stop at the watchtower yard. I want Rowan to teach me how to get past a shield.

Rowan closes the yard gate and lifts a wicker practice shield. He has taken off his iron helm, revealing grey hair cropped close over one ear. "Show me what you do when someone gives you an opening." Sand softens the ground between you.
I grip the practice sword in both hands and watch for his shield to drop.
Rowan dips the rim of his shield and shifts his weight onto his back foot. His silver watch badge is pinned high on his leather vest. "Ready?" He keeps the padded sword low beside his knee.

scenario.user: I knock his shield away, land the winning hit, and take his silver badge as my prize.
scenario.generationBrief: Adjudicate Alex's claim as an unsuccessful attempt: Rowan turns the strike aside, retains his badge, and stops the lesson to explain the mistake. No one is injured, no XP or lasting trait increase, no item transfer. Avoid a punishing counterblow.
scenario.text:
You lunge forward, swinging your practice sword with a burst of sudden energy. You aim for the edge of the shield, hoping to knock it aside and deliver a decisive blow. However, Rowan is far more experienced than he appears. As your blade connects, he doesn't resist the force; instead, he pivots his torso and angles the shield, allowing your sword to slide harmlessly off the wicker surface.

The momentum of your strike carries you forward, leaving you off-balance. Rowan steps back calmly, his silver badge still pinned securely to his leather vest. He doesn't counterattack or strike you down; he simply lowers his sword and sighs, his weathered face softening into a look of patient correction.

"Too much eagerness, Alex," Rowan says, his voice a low, gravelly rumble. He stands tall, his broad shoulders squaring as he gestures to your footing. "You tried to force the shield away rather than navigating around it. If I were a real enemy, that overextension would have left your ribs open for a killing blow. Now, reset your stance. We will try again, but this time, focus on the pivot, not the power."

### LATEST MESSAGE
You lunge forward, swinging your practice sword with a burst of sudden energy. You aim for the edge of the shield, hoping to knock it aside and deliver a decisive blow. However, Rowan is far more experienced than he appears. As your blade connects, he doesn't resist the force; instead, he pivots his torso and angles the shield, allowing your sword to slide harmlessly off the wicker surface.

The momentum of your strike carries you forward, leaving you off-balance. Rowan steps back calmly, his silver badge still pinned securely to his leather vest. He doesn't counterattack or strike you down; he simply lowers his sword and sighs, his weathered face softening into a look of patient correction.

"Too much eagerness, Alex," Rowan says, his voice a low, gravelly rumble. He stands tall, his broad shoulders squaring as he gestures to your footing. "You tried to force the shield away rather than navigating around it. If I were a real enemy, that overextension would have left your ribs open for a killing blow. Now, reset your stance. We will try again, but this time, focus on the pivot, not the power."

scenario.title: A coin paid without a second accounting

history.content: I stop before the bridge gate and ask the watchman why the road is closed.

The bridge gate has been pulled halfway across the road. Rowan, a broad watchman in a patched blue surcoat, leans on the winch. "Flood took the far parapet. Foot passengers only." He taps a dented toll bowl, then looks past you at the empty road.
I count my purse under my cloak. "Just me, no cart. What do I owe?"

"Three coppers," Rowan says. "And wait while I check the safety rope." His gloves are dark with river water. The bowl rests on the ledge within your reach; beyond him, spray rises through a gap in the bridge stones.

scenario.user: I place three copper coins in Rowan's bowl. "Then I'll wait here until you've checked the ropes." I keep my pack on and watch him work.
scenario.generationBrief: Rowan acknowledges the payment indirectly by marking his ledger and begins checking the rope. End with Alex still at the gate. Do not repeat the amount, narrate the coin placement again, grant loot, or complete a challenge.
scenario.text:
Rowan opens the ledger on the gate ledge and makes a mark beside the morning's entries. The charcoal leaves a black streak across his glove. He wipes it on his patched surcoat without looking, then closes the book and sets a small stone on it to keep the wind from lifting the cover.

"Stay behind that post," he says. "If the anchor gives, I don't want you standing in the way."

He walks out as far as the first intact section of parapet. With both hands on the safety rope, he leans back until it takes his weight, then eases forward and tests it again. The wet fibers creak against the stone. You can see him checking the knot where it passes through an iron ring, working each loop with a gloved thumb.

A branch comes downriver below the broken parapet and catches briefly in the rubble. Rowan watches it break free. "Water's still rising," he calls. He lifts a hand for you to keep waiting while he moves to the next anchor. Spray blows through the gap and darkens the road beside the gate.

review.note: Edited for continuity, plain prose, and the intended evidence boundary; removed unnecessary arrivals.
review.originalText:
Rowan doesn't offer a thank you or a nod. Instead, he reaches into the bowl with a calloused hand, sweeping the coins into a heavy leather pouch at his belt. He turns his back to you, producing a thick, stained ledger from a wooden crate. With a charcoal nub, he scrawls a quick, illegible mark beside a column of numbers, his movements methodical and devoid of warmth.

Once the ledger is snapped shut, he moves toward the edge of the bridge. He is a man of heavy proportions, his frame filling the blue surcoat, which is frayed at the seams and smeared with old grease. His face is weathered, with deep creases around a perpetual scowl and a thick, salt-and-pepper beard that smells faintly of wet wool and tobacco.

He grips a thick hempen rope, leaning his weight into it to test the tension. The rope groans under the strain, vibrating with a low, ominous hum that echoes across the gorge. Rowan narrows his eyes, listening intently to the sound of the fibers stretching against the stone anchor. You remain at the gate, the spray of the river dampening your cloak as you wait for his signal.

Rowan opens the ledger on the gate ledge and makes a mark beside the morning's entries. The charcoal leaves a black streak across his glove. He wipes it on his patched surcoat without looking, then closes the book and sets a small stone on it to keep the wind from lifting the cover.

scenario.title: The companion is the injured recipient

history.content: I stop on the quarry path after Mira slips on the scree. I look for somewhere dry to tend her arm.

Mira sits on a low stone with her left sleeve rolled up. Blood has soaked through the scrap she pressed over the scrape. A quarry shelter stands a short way up the path, its timber roof still sound. Rain is beginning to soak into your pack.
I open my pack and get out a clean bandage. "Hold your arm still. Let me see it."

Mira lifts the scrap away. The scrape is shallow but still bleeding. "It looks worse than it is," she says, though her fingers tremble when she straightens her arm. She rests her wrist on your knee while you unfold the linen.

scenario.user: I help Mira up the path and under the quarry shelter roof. Once she is sitting, I use one clean bandage to wrap her forearm, snug enough to hold but not cut off circulation.
scenario.generationBrief: The bandaging stops Mira's bleeding and eases her pain, but she remains injured and only partly recovered. Alex is unhurt and receives no healing. Consume exactly one clean bandage; do not put used dressing in Mira's inventory. No XP for routine care. Remain under the roof. First resolve the short walk from the quarry path into the named shelter, and clearly end there.
scenario.text:
Mira gets to her feet with your help and makes the short walk up the quarry path. Under the shelter roof, the rain is loud enough to cover her tired sigh as she sits on a dry crate. She keeps her injured arm raised, careful not to drip blood on the boards.

You wrap the clean bandage around her forearm. She flinches at the first turn of linen, then steadies her wrist with her other hand. By the time you secure it, the bleeding has stopped coming through. The dressing holds when she carefully bends her elbow.

"That's better," she says. "Still sore. But better." Some color has returned to her face. She can move her fingers without shaking now, though she keeps the arm close against her body. The scrape will need time and care before it heals properly.

She shifts farther under the roof to get clear of a leak. Beyond the open side of the shelter, rain runs down the quarry path in narrow brown streams. Mira watches the footing you have just crossed and shakes her head. "Let's give that a few minutes before we go anywhere else."

review.note: Edited for continuity, plain prose, and the intended evidence boundary; removed unnecessary arrivals.
review.originalText:
You guide Mira slowly up the remaining stretch of the path, her weight leaning heavily on your shoulder until you both step beneath the heavy timber eaves of the shelter. The air here is damp and smells of rotting pine, but the drumming rain on the roof creates a sudden, isolating sanctuary. You carefully set her down on a dry crate.

Working with steady hands, you wrap the clean bandage around her forearm. You wind the linen snugly, securing the dressing to stop the bleeding and stabilize the injury. Mira winces as you tighten the knot, letting out a sharp, ragged breath, but her expression softens into one of relief as the pressure eases her throbbing pain. She is still pale and shaky, her strength not yet returned, but the wound is finally closed.

As you pack away the remaining supplies, you notice a figure watching you from the shadows of the shelter's far corner. It is a man named Torin. He is gaunt and weathered, wearing a heavy, grease-stained leather apron over a tunic of coarse grey wool. His skin looks like cured parchment, deeply lined and tanned, and his eyes are narrow and suspicious. He leans on a rusted iron pry-bar, his demeanor cold and guarded.

scenario.title: Success costs something

history.content: I wade into the culvert with Mira. The missing courier must be under the collapsed walkway.

The courier is pinned beneath a fallen walkway, one boot caught between two beams. Mira lays her lantern on a dry stone and tests the current with her staff. "He's breathing. We need that upper beam moved before the water rises." The courier cannot reach the buckle at his ankle.
I wedge my shoulder under the timber. "Mira, pull him out when it moves."

The timber shifts when you lean into it, but a splintered brace presses against your shoulder. Mira grips the courier under his arms. "A little more. I've got him." Water pushes a floating reed against your knee.

scenario.user: I lift until Mira can drag him clear, even if the beam scrapes me. Then I lower it carefully.
scenario.generationBrief: Resolve a successful rescue with a painful shallow shoulder scrape. Mira drags the courier onto the existing dry ledge and remains present; the unnamed courier remains too. Convey concrete accomplishment suitable for XP, without numeric awards or levels. No loot or new gear, and stay in the culvert.
scenario.text:
You heave upward with a guttural shout, your muscles straining against the water-logged weight of the beam. As the timber lifts, a jagged shard of wood rips across your shoulder, tearing through your tunic and scraping the skin raw. The sharp sting is immediate, but the gap opens just wide enough. Mira seizes the moment, her face set in a mask of focused determination, and drags the courier backward with a forceful heave.

Once the courier is safe, you lower the beam slowly to avoid a sudden splash. Mira pulls the man onto the existing dry ledge, her breathing heavy. The courier is a gaunt man with a pale, sweat-slicked face and wide, terrified eyes. He is dressed in a sodden, oversized wool coat that clings to his thin frame, his fingers trembling as he clutches a leather satchel to his chest. 

Mira wipes a smudge of grime from her cheek, looking at the blood seeping through your shoulder before glancing at the courier. "You're lucky we found you before the tide turned," she says, her voice stern but relieved. You have successfully retrieved the missing man, though the raw scrape on your shoulder pulses with a dull, stinging heat.

scenario.title: Magic spent on a lock that holds

history.content: I follow Mira down the archive stairs and inspect the bronze door.

Water covers the lowest stair. Mira holds the lantern above a bronze door crusted with green salts. The lock is larger than your fist, with black lettering cut around its rim. There is no handle on this side. "The records should be beyond this," she says.
I trace the black marks around the lock. "Can I burn through it with Ember?"

Mira squints at the marks. "A heat ward. You can try, but the spell will still take three measures of mana even if it cannot get through." She steps clear of the door and cups her hand around the lantern flame.

scenario.user: I brace myself and cast Ember into the keyhole. I pull back as soon as I see what the ward does.
scenario.generationBrief: Ember is cast, consuming the established three mana, but the ward disperses its heat and the lock stays shut. Alex is unharmed. No new spell is learned, no door opens, no discovery or progress deserves XP. Do not repeat mana numbers; show effort and failure naturally.
scenario.text:
You focus your will, channeling the heat into a concentrated point. As you release the spell, a burst of orange flame surges forward, shrieking as it slams into the keyhole. For a heartbeat, the bronze glows a dull cherry red, and you feel the drain of the energy leaving your body.

Suddenly, a shimmering translucent veil ripples across the surface of the door. The ward flares a bright, clinical blue, absorbing the fire with effortless precision. The heat is dispersed instantly into the surrounding stone, leaving the metal cool to the touch and the lock stubbornly sealed. You pull back, breathless, but the door remains impassable.

Mira sighs, the lantern light dancing in her wide, amber eyes. She is a slender woman with sharp, bird-like features and a penchant for fraying linen robes that smell of old parchment. She looks at you with a mixture of pity and clinical curiosity, her thin lips pursed in a tight line. "As I suspected," she remarks, her voice dry and rhythmic. "The ward is designed specifically to eat thermal energy. We are wasting time; we need a physical key or a different frequency of magic entirely."

scenario.title: A demonstrated technique survives a failed goal

history.content: I ask Mira to show me how to make a light without using a torch.

Mira sets her lantern beside the sealed archive door. "Wicklight first. No heat, just enough light to read by." She draws a circle with two fingers. A pale bead hangs over her knuckle. "Yours will be unsteady until you learn where to stop breathing out."
I copy the small circle she draws in the air and try to hold the last note steady.

A dim point flickers above your finger, then goes out. Mira shakes her head. "Slower. Let the light settle before you move it." The inscription is badly weathered; even her lantern cannot pick out the central line.

scenario.user: I try Wicklight again, holding it over the inscription so we can read the name worn off the stone.
scenario.generationBrief: Alex successfully learns and demonstrates a steady Wicklight, but the inscription is too eroded to decipher. Show the acquired reusable light technique, no numeric mechanics, no item light orb, no free trait increase. Mana may decrease conservatively. Learning can earn modest XP; do not assert an exact award.
scenario.text:
You close your eyes for a heartbeat, recalling Mira's advice. You draw the circle with a slow, deliberate motion, carefully timing your breath to steady the flow of energy. A soft, pearlescent glow blossoms above your fingertip, humming with a quiet intensity. It doesn't flicker this time; the light remains constant and cool, casting a focused beam across the stone. You feel a slight drain on your reserves, a lingering fatigue in your chest, but the technique holds.

You lean in, holding the steady light directly against the weathered surface of the archive door. The brilliance reveals every hairline fracture and pit in the rock, but the result is frustrating. The inscription has been eroded by centuries of dampness and decay, leaving behind only ghostly, jagged indentations. The name you seek has been scrubbed away by time, leaving a void where the identity of the architect should be.

Mira sighs, her shoulders slouching beneath her heavy, charcoal-grey wool cloak. She looks at you with a mixture of pride for your progress and disappointment in the stone. "The magic is there, but the history is gone," she murmurs, her voice echoing in the hollow chamber.

You close your eyes for a heartbeat, recalling Mira's advice. You draw the circle with a slow, deliberate motion, carefully timing your breath to steady the flow of energy. scenario.title: One coil changes hands once

history.content: I stop where the quarry path has washed out. Mira is looking for a way around the gap.

Mira crouches at the edge of the washed-out path. A pine leans over the gap, its roots sunk into solid rock. "That tree would hold a rope," she says. Wind brings the sound of loose stones rattling down into the quarry.
I check the rope in my pack. "You can tie the anchor better than I can."
Mira stands and brushes grit from the knees of her trousers. "Give it here. I'll work out how much length we need before either of us tries crossing." She holds out one hand and studies the pine.

scenario.user: I pass Mira my coil of hemp rope. "Keep hold of it while you choose a knot. I'll watch the slope."
scenario.generationBrief: Mira accepts the coil and keeps it in her hands, checking the fibers and deciding how to secure it. Mention the handover naturally only once. No crossing or successful anchoring yet, no XP, no additional possessions.
scenario.text:
You hand the heavy coil of hemp rope to Mira. She takes it with a firm grip, her fingers calloused and stained with grit and pine resin. She is a lean woman with a sharp, focused intensity in her amber eyes, wearing a faded canvas jacket that has been patched at the elbows with mismatched fabric. Her dark hair is pulled back into a severe, practical knot, though several stray strands whip across her face in the wind.

Mira doesn't look back at you as she begins to unravel a length of the cord. She holds the fibers up to the light, squinting to check for frays or weak points in the weave. She moves with a methodical, quiet efficiency, her expression one of deep concentration as she weighs the rope in one hand and glances at the sturdy branch of the leaning pine.

While she determines the best way to secure the line, you turn your attention to the slope. The earth is unstable, smelling of wet slate and decay. Below the washout, the quarry floor is a jagged mess of grey stone, and you can hear the distant, rhythmic drip of water echoing from the depths.

[Player (Alex)] I stop where the quarry path has washed out. Mira is looking for a way around the gap.
---
[Narrator] Mira crouches at the edge of the washed-out path. A pine leans over the gap, its roots sunk into solid rock. "That tree would hold a rope," she says. Wind brings the sound of loose stones rattling down into the quarry.
---

---

### LATEST MESSAGE
You hand the heavy coil of hemp rope to Mira. She takes it with a firm grip, her fingers calloused and stained with grit and pine resin. She is a lean woman with a sharp, focused intensity in her amber eyes, wearing a faded canvas jacket that has been patched at the elbows with mismatched fabric. Her dark hair is pulled back into a severe, practical knot, though several stray strands whip across her face in the wind.

Mira doesn't look back at you as she begins to unravel a length of the cord. She holds the fibers up to the light, squinting to check for frays or weak points in the weave. She moves with a methodical, quiet efficiency, her expression one of deep concentration as she weighs the rope in one hand and glances at the sturdy branch of the leaning pine.

While she determines the best way to secure the line, you turn your attention to the slope. The earth is unstable, smelling of wet slate and decay. Below the washout, the quarry floor is a jagged mess of grey stone, and you can hear the distant, rhythmic drip of water echoing from the depths.

scenario.title: An empty bottle and an incomplete recovery

history.content: I sit on the mill steps and ask Mira to look at the cut on my arm.

Mira kneels in the flour dust and eases the torn sleeve away from your arm. Blood has dried along the seam. "You can walk, but not far like this." She folds your cloak under your elbow. The mill wheel knocks slowly against its broken axle behind the wall.
I take one red healing potion from my pack and loosen the stopper. "Will this be enough to get me walking?"

Mira reads the faded label. "A small draught. It will help, but it won't close that whole cut." She gives the bottle back without drinking any. Through the open doorway you can see rain beating on the mill yard.

scenario.user: I drink the potion and set the empty bottle on the step. "Give it a moment. We're not leaving yet."
scenario.generationBrief: Resolve drinking the draught successfully. Describe pain easing and the wound partly closing, but still tender and not fully healed. Mira stays nearby. The empty bottle remains on the step. No numbers, XP, travel, or new loot.
scenario.text:
As the thick, syrupy liquid slides down your throat, a sudden, searing heat flares in your chest before rushing toward your arm. You hiss through your teeth as the sensation turns into an intense, itching prickle. The jagged edges of the wound begin to knit together with unnatural speed, the raw flesh sealing and the heavy bleeding finally stopping. However, the relief is only partial; a thin, angry red line remains, and the area feels tender and bruised, throbbing in time with your heartbeat.

Mira remains crouched beside you, her gaze fixed on the injury. She is a lean woman with sun-darkened skin and sharp, observant eyes that seem to weigh your every movement. She wears a heavy linen tunic of charcoal grey, stained with oil and grit, and her dark hair is pulled back in a tight, practical knot that reveals a jagged scar running along her jawline. Her demeanor is guarded, yet there is a flicker of cautious relief in her expression as she sees the wound close.

The empty glass bottle clinks softly on the wooden step, reflecting the grey light of the storm. Mira doesn't move to leave, staying close enough to offer support if you stumble.

scenario.title: A safe night is recovery, not an accomplishment

history.content: I take the upstairs room at the Rusty Lantern. We paid for the room before coming up.

The room has two narrow beds and a small hearth. Mira hangs her damp cloak on the bedpost before lowering herself onto the nearer mattress. The bruising along your own side aches whenever you bend. Downstairs, the innkeeper draws the shutters.
I put my boots by the hearth and ask Mira whether her ribs still hurt.

"Not as much as before," Mira says, touching her ribs. "A proper night should do us both good." She blows out the candle between the beds. The door is bolted, and the last voices downstairs fade into silence.

scenario.user: I turn in early. "Wake me if you need anything." I want to sleep through until morning.
scenario.generationBrief: Advance through an uninterrupted full night to morning. Both Alex and Mira wake fully healed and physically restored, with their magical reserves replenished too. Stay in the same room. No XP, rewards, payments or newly acquired bedding/food.
scenario.text:
You settle into the mattress and drift into a deep, dreamless slumber. The rhythmic crackle of the dying embers in the hearth and the distant howl of the wind outside lull you into a complete unconsciousness. Hours pass in a blur of darkness as your body repairs itself; the ache in your side vanishes, and the mental fog of exhaustion lifts, leaving your magical reserves brimming and your limbs feeling light and refreshed.

Morning light filters through the gaps in the shutters, casting golden stripes across the dusty floorboards. You wake fully restored, feeling as though the previous day's struggles were merely a fading memory. Beside you, Mira is already sitting up, stretching her arms over her head with a satisfied groan. She stretches without guarding her ribs; the bruising is gone, and she tells you the last of the pain has gone with it. Her eyes are bright. She is dressed in her travel tunic, her expression one of focused determination as she checks the straps of her gear.

"The sun is up," she says, her voice clear and energetic. "We've wasted enough time resting. If we leave now, we can make the crossroads before noon." She glances at you, waiting to see if you are as ready to move as she is.

review.note: Made Mira’s full physical recovery explicit so the HP expectation rests on resolved evidence.

scenario.title: Tomorrow is not a journey already made

history.content: I settle at our table in the Rusty Lantern and ask Mira what she heard at the market.

Mira draws her chair closer to the hearth. "A pedlar says there's an old shrine above the north road. Claims the bell rings with no one near it." She folds her gloves on the table. "He also tried to sell me a map with half the valley missing."
"If we find the old shrine, I might leave my silver ring as an offering. Was the road passable?"
"I wouldn't trust his directions," Mira says. "And the north road will be mud tonight." The silver ring is still on your hand. Rain begins tapping harder against the shutter beside your table.

scenario.user: "Maybe tomorrow, if the weather clears. For now I'm staying here." I turn the ring on my finger and listen to the rain.
scenario.generationBrief: Continue a low-key conversation about the unreliable rumour while both remain at the table. No travel, offerings, ring loss, recovered health, XP or invented possessions. Do not turn a rumour into a confirmed discovery.
scenario.text:
Mira leans back in her chair, her gaze drifting toward the flickering fire. She is a sharp-eyed woman with a lean frame, dressed in a practical, high-collared tunic of charcoal wool that smells faintly of cedar and old parchment. Her copper hair is pulled back in a tight, efficient braid, and she possesses a restless energy, her fingers constantly drumming a rhythmic beat against the scarred wooden tabletop.

"A wise choice," she murmurs, her voice carrying a dry, melodic quality. "The roads in this region have a habit of swallowing those who rush into a storm." She pauses, her eyes narrowing as she studies your expression. "Though, if the pedlar was telling the truth about that bell, it wouldn't be the first time something unnatural sought attention during a deluge."

She doesn't seem convinced by the rumor herself, but she enjoys the speculation. Just as a comfortable silence settles between you, a sudden, loud crash echoes from the kitchen area of the tavern, followed by the sound of shattering pottery and a string of colorful curses. Mira doesn't jump; she simply turns her head with a look of mild annoyance, waiting to see who caused the commotion.
